column2: Then one should go to Phalgu-tirtha, supreme, situated in the great river; from Naga, from Janardana, from the well, and from the banyan and Uttara-manasa.
This is called the Gaya-head; it is called Phalgu-tirtha; Mundaprishtha, Naga and the others — the essence, then the inner essence,
in which Shri, or the cow, the wish-cow, water and earth bear fruit; since vision, loveliness and the rest — Phalgu-tirtha is not "insubstantial."
A man who bathes at Phalgu-tirtha and sees the god Gadadhara — what is not obtained by this for men who do good deeds?
The sacred places on earth and the lakes up to the ocean will go to Phalgu-tirtha once a day, every day.
At Phalgu-tirtha, the king of sacred places, one who bathes with reverence attains Brahma's world for the ancestors and enjoyment and liberation for himself.
Having bathed, the performer of ancestral rites, the giver of pinda, should then bow to the god Pitamaha: "In the Kali age the people are Maheshvaras; here the Goddess and Gadadhara;
Pitamaha in linga form — I bow to that Maheshvara; Gadadhara, Bala, Kama, Aniruddha, Narayana,
Brahma, Vishnu, Narasimha by name, Varaha and the rest I bow." Then having seen Gadadhara one lifts a hundred families.
On the second day, Dharmaranya in the excellent hermitage of Matanga: having bathed in the Matanga-step-well one becomes a giver of the ancestral rite and pinda.
Having bowed to Matangesha and Suddhesha, one should say: "Be witnesses, gods and guardians of the world:
having come to this Matanga I have made atonement for the ancestors." Bathing, libation, ancestral rites and so on at Brahma-tirtha, and at the well,
between the elbow and the sacrificial post, the ancestral rite lifts a hundred families. Having bowed to the Mahabodhi tree, the righteous shares heaven.
On the third day one of controlled vows should bathe in Brahma-sara: "I bathe at the Brahma-sara sacred place for prosperity of Brahma,

for the ancestors' Brahma-world, frequented by hosts of Brahma-sages." The performer of the ancestral rite should give the libation, pinda, and sprinkling; and the seeker of the Vajapeya should circumambulate the Brahma post.
A sage alone, with pot and kusha tip in hand, gives water at the root of a mango; the mango is watered and the ancestors satisfied — one act is famed as doing two purposes.
Having bowed to Brahma one lifts a hundred families. On the fourth day at Phalgu-tirtha, having bathed and made libation to gods and others,
one should have the ancestral rite with pinda done at Gayashiras. Gaya field is five krosha; Gayashiras one krosha.
There by giving pinda one lifts a hundred families. At Mundaprishtha the wise Mahadeva placed his foot.
At Mundaprishtha the head is directly called Gayashiras; directly there Gayashiras made a hermitage at Phalgu-tirtha.
Nectar flows there; what is given to ancestors is imperishable. Having bathed at Dashashvamedha and seen the god Pitamaha,
having touched Rudrapada, a man is not born again here. Having given a pinda the size of a shami leaf at Gayashiras,
those in hell go to heaven and those in heaven attain liberation. With pudding, flour, barley meal and porridge,
the giving of pinda with rice, wheat mixed with sesame; having given pinda at Rudrapada one lifts a hundred families.
Likewise at Vishnupada the giver of pinda is freed from debt; a man saves a hundred families of father and others and himself.
Likewise at Brahmapada the performer leads the ancestors to Brahma's world; likewise at Dakshinagni-pada and Garhapatya-pada;
at the foot of the Ahavaniya the performer obtains the fruit of sacrifice; of the Avasathya, the Moon, the Sun and the host,
of Agastya and Kartikeya the performer saves his family. Having bowed to the Sun's chariot a man should bow to Karnaditya;
having bowed to Kanakesha-pada, he should bow to Gayakedaraka; freed from all sins he leads the ancestors to Brahma's city.
Vishala also, at Gayashiras, became a giver of pinda and had a son. In Vishala, Vishala the prince said to the Brahmins:
How shall I have sons and the rest? The Brahmins said to Vishalaka: "By giving pinda at Gaya all will be yours."
Vishala too gave pindas to the ancestors at Gayashiras. Then seeing in the sky white, red and dark men, he asked them:
Who are you? One, the white one, said to Vishalaka: "I am the white; your father, gone to Indra's world, of good deeds;
mine is the red, my father, son, and the dark is the grandfather; he said, having reached hell, we were freed by you.
By your giving of pinda we go to Brahma's world," so saying they went. Vishala, having obtained sons and the rest, ruled the kingdom and went to Hari.
The king of ghosts, for his own liberation, said this to a merchant: "Afflicted along with all the ghosts, the fruit of good deeds is enjoyed.
On the Shravana-dvadashi yoga a pot with food and water, given in the past at midday, stands for sustenance.
Take my wealth and go; become a giver of pinda at Gaya." The merchant took the wealth and became a giver of pinda at Gaya.
The king of ghosts with the ghosts was freed and taken to Hari's city. By giving pinda at Gayashiras to oneself and to one's ancestors,
to those in the father's line and in the mother's line likewise, the teacher's, father-in-law's and kin, and other dead relatives:

Those in my family whose pinda lapsed, without sons or wives, those who gave up rites, the blind from birth and cripples,
agnipuran:115:66	the deformed, the unborn embryos, known and unknown in my family — the pinda given by me, may it reach them imperishable.
agnipuran:115:67	Whichever of my ancestors stay in the form of ghosts, may all of them be satisfied by the giving of pinda always.
Pinda is to be given to all by all family-saviors; likewise to oneself by one desiring an imperishable world.
On the fifth day the wise one should bathe at Gadalola with the mantra: "At the mace-washing sacred place, the very purifying Gadalola,
I bathe for the peace of the disease of the world, Janardana. Homage to the Akshayavata, giver of imperishable heaven,
for the imperishability of ancestors and the destruction of all sins." One should do the ancestral rite under the banyan and feed Brahmins;
when one Brahmin is fed a crore is fed; what then of many fed? What is given to the ancestors is imperishable.
He who gives food at Gaya has his ancestors blessed with sons. Having bowed to the banyan and Vateshvara, one should worship the great-grandfather;
he obtains imperishable worlds, lifts a hundred families. The pilgrimage to Gaya, in order or out of order, is greatly fruitful.
Siddheshvara, Rudresha, Ramesha, Brahmakeshvara — having worshipped the eight secret lingas one shares all.
One should bow for fortune to Narayana, Varaha, Narasimha; Brahma-Vishnu-Mahesha by name, the destroyer of Tripura, giving all;
having worshipped Sita, Rama, Garuda and Vamana, one obtains all desires and leads the ancestors to Brahma's world.
Having worshipped the god Adi-Gadadhara with the gods, freed from the three debts, he saves his whole family.
The stone of divine form is meritorious; therefore the stone is divine. In Gaya there is no place where there is no sacred place.
Whoever's name one drops a pinda for, that leads him to eternal Brahman. Having bowed to Phalgvisha, Phalgu-chandi and Angarakeshvara,
the performer of the ancestral rite at Matanga's foot should be at Bharata's hermitage; at Hamsa-tirtha, Koti-tirtha, where is Pandushila-anna-da;
there the giver of pinda at Agnidhara, Madhusravas; one should bow to Rudresha, Kilikilesha and Vriddhi-Vinayaka;
the giver of pinda at Dhenukaranya should bow to the cow at the cow's foot; he saves all ancestors; and the giver of pinda at Sarasvati;
having performed the evening twilight prayer one should bow to the goddess Sarasvati; he becomes a Brahmin who performs the three twilights, master of Veda and Vedangas.
Having circumambulated Gaya and worshipped the Brahmins of Gaya, all done there — gift of food and the rest — becomes imperishable.
Having praised, one should pray to the god, the primal god, Gadadhara: "Gadadhara, dweller of Gaya, giver of the goal to ancestors and others,
I bow to you, giver of yoga, for dharma, wealth, desire and liberation, free of body, senses, mind, intellect, life-breath and ego,
eternally pure, endowed with intelligence, true Brahman — I bow. The god of bliss, non-dual, praised by gods and demons,
joined with hosts of gods and goddesses, I always bow; the subduer of the pain of the Kali age's stain, wearer of the forest garland,
protector of the lord of all worlds, mind bent on lifting families, whose Self is divided into manifest and unmanifest, the undivided Self in oneself,
established, most steady, the essence, I praise, crusher of terrible sin. I have come to Gaya, god, for the ancestral rite, Gadadhara;
be my witness today here; I am free of the three debts. May the gods be my witnesses, Brahma, Ishana and the rest;
having reached Gaya I have made atonement for the ancestors." By reciting the Gaya-mahatmya, at ancestral rites and the like one shares Brahma's world;
the ancestral rite of the ancestors is imperishable, giving imperishable Brahma's world.
Here the giving of scent, flowers, incense, lamp and clothing; having taken out ghee-smeared food one asks the fire: "I shall do it."
Do, being permitted, the one with fire should offer in the fire; the one without fire in the ancestor's hand with the thread, by mantra:
To Agni, bearer of offerings to ancestors, svaha the first oblation; to Soma with the ancestors, then to Yama, to Angiras, others.

Having placed the remainder of the offering in the food vessel one should touch the vessel: "Earth is your vessel, sky the cover; into the immortal mouth of the Brahmin I offer immortality, svaha"; having recited this, "This Vishnu," one should put the Brahmin's thumb in the food.
With "Apahata" having scattered sesame one should give the food; having said "Enjoy," then one should recite the Gayatri and the rest:
Homage to the gods, to the ancestors, and to the great yogis; homage to Svadha and Svaha always, homage, homage.
Knowing them satisfied one should scatter food, give water time after time; having recited the Gayatri as before one should recite "Madhu, madhu."
One should ask "Are you satisfied?" and they should say "We are satisfied." Having obtained leave for the remaining food, all the food together
having taken up at the side of the leavings and having done the washing, one should give three pindas on the kusha; others say after they have rinsed.
After they have rinsed, one should give water, flowers and rice; then imperishable water; the man should pray for blessings:
I shall have svadha pronounced — he should ask and, permitted, it should be spoken: "To the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers in front,
let svadha be spoken, may there be svadha," and as it is being spoken, so; one should pour water, having set the vessel upright and on the right.
